research_brief.research_summary: Chaplin's arc is a natural three-act story: a London child in the workhouse (1896), the Tramp's debut (Kid Auto Races at Venice, 1914) and full creative control (co-founding United Artists, 1919), then exile (re-entry permit revoked, 1952) and a 12-minute standing ovation at the 1972 Oscars. He resisted talkies into the sound era, so a silent, intertitle-driven 3D piece is thematically on-brand rather than a compromise. Rights note: Bubbles Inc. controls commercial use of his name/likeness/Tramp image and Roy Export owns the films/stills — a biographical piece should evoke iconography (bowler, cane, film set) rather than replicate his likeness or footage.

data_points.claim: In 1896 Chaplin, his mother and half-brother were admitted to a London workhouse; he was in workhouses twice before age nine
The Tramp costume debuted in Kid Auto Races at Venice, released 7 February 1914
Chaplin co-founded United Artists in 1919, gaining full creative control
Chaplin kept making silent-style films into the sound era (City Lights 1931, Modern Times 1936) and wrote his own scores, including the 'Smile' melody
In September 1952, while sailing to London for Limelight's premiere, his US re-entry permit was revoked
He returned in April 1972 for an honorary Oscar and received a 12-minute standing ovation; knighted in March 1975
